children: Fast-fashion giant Shein slid in its long-awaited trading debut, as regulatory headwinds and slowing sales challenge a company once valued at about US$66 billion.
The retailer's stock fell tumbled as much as 10% in early trading in Hong Kong after an initial public offering that valued the company at roughly a quarter of its peak.
Shein's shares fell as low as 43.72 Hong Kong dollars on Tuesday before regaining some ground to trade at 44.50 Hong Kong dollars, implying a market cap of around US$24 billion.

The listing by the China-founded company famous for ultracheap, trendy apparel has been years in the making. A series of regulatory obstacles, heightened by geopolitical tensions, have hurt Shein's business and complicated efforts to go public.

Shein's circuitous path toward an IPO included attempts to list in New York and London, both of which fell through. But even with the cut-down valuation, the IPO is still one of the largest in Hong Kong so far this year, behind tech names like Nvidia supplier Zhongji Innolight and Luxshare Precision Industry, a supplier for Apple.
Shein's offering drew cornerstone investors including General Atlantic and Greenwoods Asset Management Hong Kong.
On Monday, it set its final offer price at 48.56 Hong Kong dollars after raising 13.60 billion Hong Kong dollars, equivalent to US$1.73 billion.
The stock was last down 8.5%, underperforming the Hang Seng Tech Index's 0.7% drop.
